subject: Billing impact for compressed payloads & padding tokens
messages:
From: Jordan Smith <jordan.smith@vendcorp.com>
To: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 6 Aug 2025 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Billing impact for compressed payloads & padding tokens

Hi Camila,

Quick question as we prep the SOW addendum for volume discounts: our ingestion pipeline precompresses event payloads (gzip) and applies a fixed padding header for routing (about ~120 bytes per record). When those payloads are decoded in your stack, how do you map byte-level changes to token counts for billing?

Specific asks:
- Do you count tokens before or after decompression/normalization?
- How do padding bytes that do not map to textual tokens get treated?
- If we have consistently high compression ratios (e.g., 8:1), can that be reflected in committed-unit discounts or in minimums?

Attached a small sample export and compression stats so you can see the worst-case footprints.

Thanks — Jordan
VendCorp (Billing)
[Attachment: VendCorp_Metrics.csv (CSV, 42KB)]

From: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood.com>
To: Jordan Smith <jordan.smith@vendcorp.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 6 Aug 2025 12:08:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Billing impact for compressed payloads & padding tokens

Jordan — thanks for the samples, that helps. High level answers first, then we'll follow with a few worked examples and a proposal for how to reflect compression in the VC-8421 commit.

High level:
- Tokenization point: We bill based on the tokenized input that the model runtime sees, which is after decompression and text-normalization (unicode normalization, trimming). So billing maps to model-level tokens rather than raw bytes.
- Padding bytes: If padding is non-text (binary routing headers), it is stripped before tokenization and does not directly count as tokens. If padding encodes visible characters (e.g., space characters added to reach a fixed length), those will tokenize and count.
- Compression/ratio: We don't bill on compression ratio itself, but we can structure the commit so your effective price reflects measured compression behavior. Two options: (1) commit to a smaller token SKU with a negotiated discount if average billed tokens per ingestion stay below an agreed threshold over a month, or (2) have a rolling true-up where we apply a compression credit to the following invoice based on the certified compression factor.

I'll let Kimberly add the detailed rounding/minimums math and Marissa can chime in on amendment language for the SOW. Attaching our current pricing PDF for reference.

Next steps:
1) Kimberly and I will calculate three sample invoices using the CSV you sent (worst/median/best compression).
2) We propose a pilot true-up path (monthly) while legal finalizes Annex language for a permanent discount.

Best,
Camila
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>

Thanks — adding a technical breakdown so everyone can see the arithmetic. I validated locally with the sample CSV. Short version: billing = billed_input_tokens + billed_output_tokens; tokenization occurs after decompression + normalization. Rounding/minimums rules below are what apply to VC hosted API SKU (we can carve an exception for committed deals if needed).

Tokenization and counting rules (applies to text generation & embeddings requests):
1) Preprocess: decompress -> unicode NFC normalization -> strip non-printing routing headers if marked as binary (our ingestion recognizes common gzip + custom header patterns).
2) Tokenize: we run the tokenizer on the cleaned text. Token counts are exact integers.
3) Rounding quantum: each API call is rounded up to the nearest token quantum of 128 tokens for metering granularity (this reduces invoice noise on micro-calls).
4) Minimum per-call floor: for streaming-style calls we apply a minimum charge equivalent to 64 tokens per call to cover overheads. This is separate from monthly commit minimums.

Worked example (from your CSV):
- Raw bytes post-decompress average: 1,024 bytes per record -> normalized text ~90 chars -> tokenized to 18 tokens (avg).
- Per-call quantum rounding: 18 tokens -> rounded up to 128 tokens for the call (since quantum applies per call).
- If you batch 50 records per call (recommended), the batch token total = 18*50 = 900 tokens -> rounded up to 896? Note: quantum rounding is per-call, but we also keep continuous batching that aggregates into the call size. Practical effect: batching eliminates per-call quantum tax.

Compression-credit proposal (pilot):
- Pilot period: 3 months. We measure your billed tokens (what ends up on invoices) vs. raw uncompressed token estimate (we'll agree on a signed measurement script).
- If average compression-adjusted billed tokens are <= 30% of the uncompressed estimate for the period, we apply a 12% effective discount to committed token units for the next billing cycle (applies only to tokens consumed under the committed SKU).
- If you exceed the threshold, standard committed pricing applies (no negative adjustments).

Minimum/true-up handling:
- Monthly true-up: we reconcile measured compression against the SOW baseline and apply credits as a line item.
- Legal annex: Marissa, would like to discuss a short clause that allows us to run the measurement script and define the certified compression ratio for invoicing.

Jordan — if you can confirm typical batch sizes and whether you can route batching server-side, we can produce a sample invoice for August showing both the current structure and the pilot credit.

-Kim
Head of Billing & Pricing, Redwood Inference
